author: reek
body: 200 visible against a 264-pixel scanline is the same shape small. No emulator feature is involved, because both pitches are ordinary arguments.

author: reek
body: Every source pixel carries its own row and column, so the assertion is where a pixel LANDED and not merely that something was painted. A width-stepping blit puts row 0 in the right place and every later row at r * 160 instead of r * 264, which is why row 0 is not evidence and the count over all 24 rows is.

author: reek
body: The sidebar columns, the taskbar rows and the 64 pad columns beyond the visible width are pre-filled with a sentinel and must still hold it. A blit that painted the whole panel would satisfy the landing count just as well, and the containment rows are what separate the two.

author: reek
body: The last row is the calibration and it is the reason to believe the rest: the same blit is asked for the visible pane width as the destination pitch, into a fresh panel, and the landing count is required to DISAGREE. Without it every row above would be satisfied by an instrument that could not tell the two pitches apart.

author: reek
body: Sabotaged against seed 6671C19A0F78F630 by stepping the destination rows by w: landing goes to 1 of 24, and the pane, sidebar and pad rows go to no. **The taskbar row does NOT move, and it is worth knowing why rather than reading it as a control that held.** A short-pitch blit writes no further than pixel 23 * 160 + 199, which is inside row 15 of a 264-pitch panel, so it cannot reach row 24 whatever it gets wrong. That row is a control against a blit that paints too MUCH, not against one that picks the wrong pitch, and the pad row is the one that catches the pitch on the containment side.

author: reek
body: A row has landed when its first and its last pixel are both where the stride says they should be. One of the two alone would be satisfied by a blit that got the row origin right and the run length wrong.
